query: The Co-free FeNiCrMn high-entropy alloy is derived from equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi and is intended to retain a favorable strength–ductility balance in its solidified solid-solution state, but its dynamic behavior across different temperatures and strain rates lacks a theoretical explanation. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could account for this behavior, and what controlled comparison within that regime would distinguish it? Specify predictions relative to a baseline, applicable boundaries, supporting evidence, and a falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: The Co‐free FeNiCrMn alloy’s unusual dynamic strength–ductility balance arises from a temperature‐ and strain rate–dependent shift in its deformation mechanism—from primarily dislocation glide at higher temperatures to an increased role for nano‐twinning at lower temperatures, due to a modified stacking fault energy in the absence of Co.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic solid-solution state of the Co‐free FeNiCrMn alloy (with an fcc structure as in the parent Cantor alloy)
generation.intervention: Subject specimens to controlled mechanical deformation (e.g., tensile or compression tests) while systematically varying temperature (from cryogenic to ambient/elevated ranges) and strain rate (from quasi-static to dynamic)
generation.conditions: Tests conducted within the temperature regime where the fcc phase is stable and in a strain rate window that can access both dislocation slip and twinning regimes
generation.structural_mediator: The density and distribution of stacking faults and nano-twin boundaries
generation.mechanism: Removal of Co modifies the stacking fault energy so that at lower temperatures and/or higher strain rates, the activation barrier for nano-twinning is reduced relative to dislocation glide. This leads to an increased formation of nano-twins that enhance strain hardening (strength) while retaining ductility. Conversely, at higher temperatures where thermal activation favors dislocation slip, the alloy exhibits lower strength though ductility is maintained.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline Co-containing Cantor alloy, the Co-free alloy will show a more pronounced nano-twinning structure under low-temperature and high strain rate conditions, resulting in a higher yield strength and enhanced strain hardening without a loss in ductility. At higher temperatures, both alloys will exhibit dominantly dislocation-mediated plasticity with less twin formation.
generation.baseline: The standard equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi (Cantor) alloy tested under the same deformation conditions
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies within the temperature range where the fcc structure is retained (i.e., below phase transformation or melting) and for strain rates that do not induce additional phase transitions (e.g., pressure-induced hcp transitions)
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative influence of Co removal on stacking fault energy and twin nucleation energy barriers is not fully established; thus, the magnitude of the differences in twin density and mechanical properties remains uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare and test two sets of samples: one of the Co-free FeNiCrMn alloy and one of the baseline CoCrFeMnNi alloy. Perform in situ mechanical deformation tests at a series of controlled temperatures (e.g., cryogenic ~77 K, room temperature ~300 K, and an elevated temperature below the melting point) and at varying strain rates. Use high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (TEM) or similar techniques to analyze the microstructure, specifically quantifying nano-twin density and dislocation structures during deformation.
measurements: Stress–strain curves to determine yield strength, strain hardening rates, and ductility
TEM imaging for nano-twin density and dislocation density
Indirect or direct measurements of stacking fault energy if feasible
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Co-free FeNiCrMn alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant increase in nano-twinning (or a corresponding change in deformation behavior) relative to the standard Cantor alloy under low-temperature or high strain rate conditions, or if the predicted improvements in strength–ductility balance are not observed, then the hypothesis would be falsified.

High entropy alloys (HEAs) are a new class of metallic materials composed of multiple principle elements in equal or near-equal atomic proportions [1] , [2] . They have been receiving significant research interest owing to their exceptional mechanical and functional properties; see, e.g., refs [3] – [5] . Among various reported HEAs, the equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi (Cantor alloy) [6] is a popular and important prototype of HEAs based on 3d transition metals. Within a wide range of temperature below its solidus, it usually forms a chemically disordered solid solution in face-centered cubic (fcc) structure at ambient pressure [6] – [9] . A unique mechanical characteristic of the Cantor alloy is an enhanced strength-ductility combination with decreasing temperature, while maintaining outstanding fracture toughness at cryogenic temperatures, which was demonstrated to be closely related to the formation of nano-twins and stacking faults in deformation [7] , [10] – [15] . Furthermore, due to the irreversible pressure-induced phase transition from the fcc to the hexagonal close-packed (hcp) lattice, the presence of the hcp structure was recently observed at ambient conditions [16] – [18] .
